There have been growing calls for integrated regional development particularly among crude oil producing states in the Niger Delta region with the aim of integrating the economic potentials among congruent states.
At the recent Niger Delta Economic and Investment Summit (NDEIS) organised by the Niger Delta Chamber of Commerce Industry, Trade, Mines and Agriculture (NDCCITMA) with the support of the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC) in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, the issue of a regional development was touted.
The issue was also echoed at the WPL Annual 2026 SME Conference with the theme: Harnessing Economic and Investment Opportunities Through SMEs, organised by Wider Perspectives Limited (WPL) in Yenagoa, the Bayelsa State capital.

The conference was organised in collaboration with the Bayelsa State Government through the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Investment and the Yenagoa Chamber of Commerce Industry, Mines and Agriculture (YECCIMA) to turn economic opportunities into investment opportunities.
In his keynote address, Warmate Jones Idikio, Director-General of the Yenagoa Chamber of Commerce Industry, Mines and Agriculture (YECCIMA), raised a number of issues.
Idikio spoke on the topic: Harnessing Economic & Investment Opportunities Through AfCFTA: Focus on the BAAR States (Bayelsa, Abia, Akwa Ibom & Rivers.
A lawyer by profession, Idikio is the Founder of the AfCFTA Roundtable and Vice President, Legal and Compliance of the All Africa Association for Small and Medium Enterprises (AAASME), he emphasised on how the BAAR states can use the AfCFTA model to harness their economic and investment opportunities.
The issue is critical for regional and subnational development as congruent states in Nigeria lack any form of collaborative partnership agreements to harness economic potentials and drive investments.
Idikio used the occasion to correct some misconceptions about AfCFTA, saying the continental free trade agreement is actually about increasing production, increasing processing, and increasing exportation.
It is also about making more investments, creating more employment for Africans and creating globally competitive industries.
“Let us be clear: AfCFTA is not the opportunity. AfCFTA is the platform. The real opportunity is what we build on that platform.
“The factories we establish. The value chains we connect. The goods we produce. The investments we attract. And the African markets we reach,” he stated.
According to him, the countries and regions that will soar under the AfCFTA will not be those that have more natural resources, but those that will most effectively convert their economic opportunities into investment opportunities.
Idikio said: “AfCFTA is not merely about trading more. It is about: producing more, processing more, exporting more, investing more, employing more Africans, and creating globally competitive industries
“The countries and regions that will win under AfCFTA will not necessarily be those with the most natural resources, but those that most effectively convert economic opportunities into investment opportunities.”

He challenged the BAAR states to see the opportunities inherent in the AfCFTA as a call to action in order to leverage on their regional advantage to continental competitiveness.
Idikio posed a question: “Today, we ask: How can BAAR turn regional advantage into continental competitiveness?”
Talking about the BAAR states, he said: “When they say we are failures, some people say this system is not working. It is an insult to us as a people, but of course let me give you simple instances.
“Number one, N40 trillion, that is the combined GDP of Bayelsa, Akwa-ibom, Abia and Rivers states, roughly $28 billion. That is the kind of value that is circulating within these four states.
“Did you know that? What did we do with it? What have we been doing with that value that is in our system? So, we’re talking about harnessing economic and investment opportunities.
“Why does this conversation matter? We’re talking about the AfCFTA. AfCFTA is Africa right? And we mentioned 1.4 billion people.”
With AfCFTA, Africa is entering a new economic era and is creating a market of over 1.4 billion people with a combined GDP exceeding US$3.4 trillion and it is the world’s largest free trade area by the number of participating countries.
He stressed that the continental trade area is a platform for regional industrialisation and value chain development.
Idikio mentioned the absence of key demographics in the four states, saying: “Nigeria has 220 million people. The combined population of these four states we don’t know, but the point is that there are opportunities these four states have that we can harness.
“How well have we gone? We don’t know. Let me make it clear that we have very clear opportunities.”
He went on to distinguish economic opportunity and investment opportunity, saying: “We talked about economic opportunity and investment opportunity. Is there a difference?
“There is a difference between economic opportunity and investment opportunity. Economic opportunity is any opportunity that creates economic value.
“So, let’s say people go into business without knowing if what they are pursuing is an economic opportunity.
“It is easy to grow cassava, but the economic opportunities around cassava are what we need to invest in. What does cassava give? Is it just fufu?
“But then, it goes beyond that. If you’re producing starch from cassava that’s the economic opportunity around cassava. And we must understand that that’s why businesses fail because they don’t see the economic opportunity for investing. It’s very important. Businesses must know that clearly.
“Let’s give a clear instance. If there is export demand, that’s an economic opportunity. It is that opportunity you invest in.”
He said examples of investment opportunities in the BAAR states include export demand, industrialisation, regional markets, logistics, digital trade, tourism, services, and “These are opportunities where capital can be invested to generate returns.”
He elaborated that for there to be industrialisation, there must be factories, industrial parks, export terminals, logistics hubs, warehouses, processing plants and technology platforms
Idikio pointed out that economic opportunity gives rise to commercial opportunity, which gives to investment opportunity and then on to trust and export.
“So, if there’s industrialisation, you know there must be factories and industrial parks. I believe that the relationship is that if there’s economic opportunity, it gives rise to commercial opportunity, which gives rise to investment opportunity, which gives rise to trust, which gives rise to export,” he stated.
He noted that though the continental trade agreement works elsewhere, it is dead in Nigeria though the government is expected to make revenue from it when there is economic growth.
Idikio referred to other successful free trade areas elsewhere in the world including the European Union with an integrated market, automotive clusters, and logistics corridors.
Another successful free trade area is USMCA among the United States, Mexico and Canada which boasts manufacturing integration and automotive value chains.
Yet another is the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) which has regional production networks and is globally known for electronics, semiconductors and automotive hubs.
He explained that while other nations are taking advantage of their regional trade areas to boost production and export, Nigeria and the BAAR states are yet to take advantage of their abundant resources to turn the corner.
Bayelsa, Abia, Akwa Ibom and Rivers states possess enormous resources including deep seaports, oil and gas resources, agricultural potential, manufacturing capacity, entrepreneurial population, strategic Atlantic coastline, access to Central Africa, and existing industrial assets.
Idikio said BAAR is strategically positioned and has the potential to become Nigeria’s South-South/South-East export and industrial corridor.
To build the BAAR regional value chain means integrating Bayelsa’s energy, marine economy and aquaculture; Rivers’ ports, petrochemicals and logistics; Abia’s manufacturing, leather industry and SMEs; and Akwa Ibom’s deep seaport, industrial processing, export logistics into one integrated regional production network capable of serving the entire African market.
Speaking of the resources, he said “These things are already there, who is investing in them?
“So between us as a state, what should we prioritise? The priority is very important; that is to talk about business, business, business.
“The government must be in the business of aggregating all of these things: is it important for all these four states to have an export processing zone? Is it important for us to have a regional logistics corridor where the trailers park?
“Do we have a container depot in Bayelsa? Is there any container depot in Akwa Ibom? We fail to ask ourselves this question, but these are opportunities.
“That is why a regional platform is very important. So, what do I ask for? The government is not here, but it is important for everyone to understand. If these four states can do something for us to develop economically then one thing you should do is to have a regional development council. Without that we cannot aggregate as we should do and development will not be sure,” he concluded.
But, with each BAAR state prioritising its own economic and investment agenda, will they ever see the need for a regional development council to drive a shared prosperity agenda?
That, obviously, is the question that the governments of Bayelsa, Abia, Akwa Ibom and Rivers states must wrap their heads around to turn their economic opportunities into investment opportunities.
